abstract: Ribosomes synthesize protein in all cells. Maintaining both the correct number and composition of ribosomes is critical for protein homeostasis. To address this challenge, cells have evolved intricate quality control mechanisms during assembly to ensure only correctly matured ribosomes are released into the translating pool. However, these assembly-associated quality control mechanisms do not deal with damage that arises during their exceptionally long lifetimes, and might equally compromise their function, or lead to reduced ribosome numbers. Recent work has revealed that ribosomes with damaged ribosomal proteins can be repaired by release of the damaged protein, thereby ensuring ribosome integrity at a fraction of the energetic cost of producing new ribosomes, appropriate for stress conditions. In this review we will cover the types of ribosome damage that are known so far, and then review the known repair mechanisms, before surveying the literature for possible additional instances of repair.
